newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Foreign firms warmer on Kazakh investment outlook.
newsitem.headline: Foreign firms warmer on Kazakh investment outlook.

text.p: Resource-rich Kazakhstan is now an exciting investment prospect but the ex-Soviet state has still some way to go in improving the business climate, participants at an investment conference said on Friday.

"This is a sound place to invest," said Richard Smith, vice-president of U.S. Citibank N.A.'s operations in Kazakhstan. "If we're willing to put our own money in, that's the best evidence there can be."
Kazakhstan is pulling out the stops to attract foreign companies to the remote tract of desert and steppe the size of western Europe.

The government has pushed forward a breathless sell-off of large state enterprises, unprecedented for a former Soviet republic, where stakes in oil and gas enterprises, telecoms and other plums are being sold for billions of dollars.
The proud Kazakhs see themselves ahead of their former Soviet neighbours in market reform.

President Nursultan Nazarbayev said on Thursday Kazakhstan was second only to Hungary in eastern Europe in investment per capita of its 16.9 million population, with six billion dollars in foreign direct investment since independence in 1991.
The English language school in Almaty is having to race to keep up with demand for new places while rents have rocketed as more western executives pile in.
But persistent problems with corruption, bureaucracy and the country's remote location mean the investment jury is still out on Kazakhstan.
"There is still a lot to do to meet demand for a better investment climate," Dulat Kuanyshev, director of the Kazakh government's investment committee, told Reuters.
"The most painful part of reform is the corruption and bureaucracy but we will fight this," Kuanyshev said.
Honouring contracts was of major concern to investors in a May survey on investment climate in Kazakhstan carried out by the Washington-based International Tax and Investment Centre.
The report cited one businessman as saying, "Unilateral cancellation of contracts is not a good thing."

Swiss-Swedish ABB AG Power Consortium Ltd suddenly lost in May a $1.4 billion deal to manage Kazakhstan's electricity grid and a framework agreement with Deutsche Telekom AG worth over a billion dollars fell apart in January.

"We're aware of some of these situations," said Citibank's Smith. "The most important thing is that there be a level playing field for all investors," he said, underlining the importance of clear legal and tax reforms.

Tatsuo Nishida, senior managing director at Japan's Sumitomo Corporation, said his company was attracted to Kazakhstan's huge reserves of oil, gas and metals and in the infrastructure projects which will follow their development.
"But getting here is still a problem," said Nishida of the far-flung Central Asian state sandwiched between Russia, China and the rest of ex-Soviet Central Asia.
"To get here, I have to fly via Moscow, Istanbul or Frankfurt," said Tokyo-based Nishida.
